abstract: Background: Secondary lymphedema is characterized by progressive lymphatic dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and tissue fibrosis, but how mechanical changes during disease progression contribute to lymphatic failure remains poorly understood. Lymphatic vessels initially undergo intraluminal pressure-induced dilation, whereas advanced disease is associated with extraluminal compression resulting from tissue remodeling. We investigated how these different mechanical stimuli affect lymphatic endothelial function. Methods and Results: We developed a human lymphatic vessel-on-chip model enabling independent control of intra- and extraluminal pressure. In contrast to vessel dilation, extraluminal compression profoundly disrupted lymphatic endothelial barrier integrity, increasing permeability and causing junctional disorganization, while also inducing a strong pro-inflammatory transcriptional response. Mechanistically, compression induced sustained intracellular Ca2 influx and activated the mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1. Piezo1 inhibition attenuated compression-induced Ca2 responses and protected endothelial barrier integrity, identifying Piezo1 as an upstream mediator of compression-induced dysfunction. Downstream, compression-induced Ca2 signaling activated Ca2 /calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), whose inhibition preserved endothelial junctional integrity and reduced both barrier dysfunction and inflammatory activation. In a murine model of secondary lymphedema, CaMKII inhibition improved lymphatic function and reduced lymphedema-associated tissue remodeling. Conclusions: These findings identify a Piezo1-CaMKII signaling axis that links pathological extraluminal compression to lymphatic endothelial dysfunction and inflammation. Targeting this pathway may help preserve lymphatic function during lymphedema progression.
